q-6840.name: Question 1
q-6840.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
q-6840.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=-\frac{3}{t\operatorname{cot}⁡t+1}.
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\,\frac{3}{(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cot}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}+1} \\  & =-\,\frac{3}{(\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot 0+1} \\  & =-\,3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

For the parametric curve x=tsin⁡t,y=3cos⁡t,−∞<t<∞, find the derivative dydx at the point P on the curve where t=π2.

a
−13π+1
b
−1π+1
c
−1
d
−3π
e
−3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula dydx=y′(t)x′(t).

Differentiating x and y, we get

x′(t)=tcos⁡t+sin⁡t,y′(t)=−3sin⁡t.

Therefore, dydx=−3sin⁡ttcos⁡t+sin⁡t=−3tcot⁡t+1. At the point where t=π2 we have dydx=−3(π2)cot⁡π2+1=−3(π2)⋅0+1=−3.

q-6816.name: Question 2
q-6816.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x={e}^{2t},\,y=({t}^{2}-1){e}^{-t},\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=1.$
q-6816.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2{e}^{2t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=(1+2t-{t}^{2}){e}^{-t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(1+2t-{t}^{2}){e}^{-t}}{2{e}^{2t}}=\frac{1}{2}(1+2t-{t}^{2}){e}^{-3t}.
$$

At the point where $t=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1}{2}(1+2(1)-(1)^{2}){e}^{-3(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1+2-1){e}^{-3} \\  & ={e}^{-3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating x and y, we get

x′(t)=2e2t,y′(t)=(1+2t−t2)e−t.

Therefore, dydx=(1+2t−t2)e−t2e2t=12(1+2t−t2)e−3t.

$$
x={t}^{3}-t,\,y={t}^{2}-4,\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=3.$
q-20987.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}-1,\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2t}{3{t}^{2}-1}.
$$

At the point where $t=3$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2\cdot 3}{3({3}^{2})-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{27-1} \\  & =\frac{3}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-6812.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=({t}^{3}-1){e}^{t},\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=0.$
q-6812.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=({t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}-1){e}^{t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

For the parametric curve (shown above)

$$
x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=\frac{\pi }{8}.$
q-20989.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}=-\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡2t.
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{8}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\,\frac{4}{3}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\  & =-\,\frac{4}{3}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-\,\frac{4}{3}\cdot 1 \\  & =-\,\frac{4}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-15476.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t})},\,y=\operatorname{cot}⁡({e}^{t}),\,-\infty <t<1,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}).$
q-15476.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t})}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{t})\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{t})}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t})}}, \\ {y}^{′}(t) & =-{e}^{t}{csc}^{2}⁡({e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{-{e}^{t}{csc}^{2}⁡({e}^{t})}{(\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{t})}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t})}})} \\  & =-\,\frac{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t})}}{{sin}^{2}⁡({e}^{t})\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{t})} \\  & =-\,\frac{2}{{sin}^{3/2}⁡({e}^{t})\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{t})}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}),$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\,\frac{2}{{sin}^{3/2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})} \\  & =-\,\frac{2}{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{3/2}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})} \\  & =-2\cdot {2}^{3/2}\,\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =-8\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We will use the formula dydx=y′(t)x′(t).

Differentiating x and y, we get

x′(t)=12sin⁡(et)⋅cos⁡(et)⋅et=etcos⁡(et)2sin⁡(et),y′(t)=−etcsc2⁡(et).

So we have dydx=−etcsc2⁡(et)(etcos⁡(et)2sin⁡(et))=−2sin⁡(et)sin2⁡(et)cos⁡(et)=−2sin3/2⁡(et)cos⁡(et).

Therefore, when t=ln⁡(π6), the slope of the tangent to the curve is dydx=−2sin3/2⁡(π6)cos⁡(π6)=−2(12)3/2(32)=−2⋅23/223=−823.

q-15477.name: Question 7
q-15477.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x={sec}^{2}⁡t,\,y={csc}^{3}⁡t,\,0<t<\frac{\pi }{2},
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
q-15477.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2{sec}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-3{csc}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{-3{csc}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t}{2{sec}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t} \\  & =-3{csc}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\,{csc}^{3}⁡t{cot}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}(\frac{1}{{sin}^{3}⁡t})(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t}){cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}(\frac{{cos}^{4}⁡t}{{sin}^{5}⁡t}) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\,\operatorname{csc}⁡t{cot}^{4}⁡t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\frac{3}{2}\,\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}){cot}^{4}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\, \\  & =-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-15457.name: Question 8
q-15457.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y={cos}^{2}⁡(t),\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6}.$
q-15457.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,{y}^{′}(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\,\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{6}) \\  & =-\,\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =-\,\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For the parametric curve 

$$
x={e}^{t}-{e}^{-t},\,y=t{e}^{t},\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=0.$
q-15470.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}+{e}^{-t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=(t+1){e}^{t}.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{(t+1){e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}+{e}^{-t}} \\  & =\frac{1+t}{1+{e}^{-2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=0,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1+0}{1+{e}^{-0}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$
